title: India's April Exports Surge to Four-Year High at $43.6 Billion, but Trade Deficit Balloons to $28.4 Billion
excerpt: Petroleum product shipments drove the breakout month even as rising crude imports and Iran-war disruption pushed the trade gap to a three-month peak.
body:
India's merchandise exports rose 13.78% year-on-year to $43.56 billion in April 2026, the strongest monthly growth in over four years, driven by a 34.66% surge in petroleum product shipments that reached $9.59 billion. But the headline was overshadowed by the import side of the ledger: total inbound goods climbed 10% to $71.94 billion, swelling the merchandise trade deficit to $28.38 billion — its highest level in three months and well above the $23.64 billion recorded in March.

| Metric | April 2026 | Year-on-Year Change | |---|---|---| | Merchandise Exports | $43.56 bn | +13.78% | | Merchandise Imports | $71.94 bn | +10% | | Trade Deficit | $28.38 bn | 3-month high | | Petroleum Exports | $9.59 bn | +34.66% | | Gold Imports | $5.63 bn | +80% | | Total Exports (incl. services) | $80.8 bn | +13.6% |

Background

Including services, the picture is somewhat brighter. Total exports — goods and services combined — hit $80.8 billion in April, up 13.6% year-on-year, with IT and business services continuing to anchor India's services surplus. Yet it is the goods gap that worries policymakers, because it feeds directly into the current account deficit and puts downward pressure on the rupee, which has already fallen to new lows against the dollar and ranks as Asia's worst-performing major currency in 2026.

What Changed

The Iran-Israel conflict is the dominant variable. India, the world's third-largest oil consumer and importer, has seen its energy import bill swell as Brent crude holds above $90. Shipments through the Middle East — historically a major trade corridor — fell 31.6% to $10.47 billion in April, reflecting both supply disruption and shipping rerouting around the Strait of Hormuz. The higher cost of longer alternative shipping routes has added an estimated 8-12% to freight rates on India-Europe and India-Middle East lanes, costs that are being passed through to exporters and importers alike.

Gold was the other notable swing factor. Imports of the precious metal jumped 80% year-on-year to $5.63 billion, reflecting both wedding-season demand and safe-haven buying amid geopolitical uncertainty. Taken together, crude oil and gold accounted for roughly half of the deficit expansion relative to March, underscoring how vulnerable India's trade balance remains to commodity-price shocks.

On the export side, the government has reason for cautious optimism. Non-petroleum and non-gems-and-jewellery exports — a cleaner measure of manufacturing competitiveness — posted solid growth, with electronics emerging as a second engine alongside refined fuels. The Commerce Ministry is targeting $1 trillion in merchandise exports by FY27 and $2 trillion in total exports by FY31, ambitions that rest on sustained MSME participation and 'Brand India' promotion in Western markets.

What This Means

For the Indian diaspora, the trade data carries practical implications. A widening current account deficit historically pressures the rupee, making remittances — which hit a record $129 billion in 2025 — cheaper to send but more expensive for recipients in real terms as domestic prices rise. NRI investors in Indian equities and real estate are watching the rupee closely: every percentage point of depreciation adds to dollar-denominated returns on the way out but erodes purchasing power for those planning eventual repatriation. The RBI's forex reserves, at roughly $640 billion, provide a buffer, but sustained deficits above $25 billion a month would test even that cushion over time.

The months ahead will hinge on two forces pulling in opposite directions: whether the Iran conflict de-escalates enough to ease crude prices, and whether India's export diversification — particularly in electronics, pharmaceuticals, and green energy components — can sustain the April momentum. The government's next trade data release in mid-June will be closely watched as a gauge of whether the April surge was structural or a one-off driven by petroleum arbitrage.
author: Diaspora Desk
